client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last year. Every time there's a family gathering coming up, I find some excuse not to go because being around everyone just makes her absence feel even more overwhelming. I'm not sure talking about it is actually going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist: It takes real courage to show up and try, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — and I want you to know that ambivalence is completely okay to bring into this space. Losing your grandmother and then facing those gatherings where her absence feels so loud sounds genuinely painful, like the people who are *there* somehow make it more vivid that she isn't. I'm curious — when you imagine yourself at one of those family events, what's the very first thought that tends to come up for you?

client: The first thought that comes up is honestly something like, "She should be here" — and then almost immediately after that, this wave of guilt because everyone else seems to be managing better than me. It's like I'm the only one still stuck, and that makes me feel even more isolated, even surrounded by family. I end up spending most of the event just going through the motions, smiling when I'm supposed to, but feeling completely hollow inside.
therapist: That thought — "she should be here" — is such a natural expression of love and loss, and it makes complete sense that it hits you hard. What strikes me is that the guilt seems to pile on top of the grief, almost like you're judging yourself for *how* you're grieving, and I wonder if that comparison to others ("everyone else is managing better") is actually something you know to be true, or more of a feeling that shows up in those painful moments. What evidence do you have that the people around you are really as "fine" as they appear?

client: I mean, when you put it that way, I guess I don't really have solid proof that everyone else is fine. It's more like... at the funeral, people seemed composed, and my cousin gave this whole speech without breaking down, and I just fell apart. But I suppose I don't actually know what's happening behind closed doors for any of them.
therapist: It sounds like you're already starting to loosen the grip of that comparison a little, which is a meaningful shift. That moment at the funeral — your cousin's composed speech versus your own tears — became a kind of "proof" in your mind, but you're recognizing now that composure on the outside doesn't tell us much about what someone carries on the inside. I'm wondering, if a close friend told you they had fallen apart at a loved one's funeral, would you see that as them being "stuck" — or as someone who loved deeply?

client: I mean... no, I wouldn't think that about a friend. I'd probably think they really loved the person they lost. But it's just different when it's me — like, I hold myself to this completely different standard and I know that's not logical, but knowing it's not logical doesn't make it stop.
therapist: You've just noticed something really important — that you *know* the double standard isn't fair, and yet the feeling persists anyway, and that gap between knowing and feeling can be one of the most frustrating parts of grief. That's actually very normal, and it doesn't mean you're broken or that therapy won't help — it just means we have some gentle work to do in helping your heart catch up to what your mind already understands. I'm curious, when you hear yourself say "it's just different when it's me," what do you think you *deserve* to feel about losing her?

client: I think I deserve to feel sad, obviously, but... I don't know if I deserve to feel this wrecked for this long. Like, it's been months and I'm still barely functioning, and part of me keeps saying I should be further along by now, that I'm being self-indulgent or something. It's easier to give other people permission to grieve than to give it to myself, I guess.
therapist: There's something quietly painful in what you just said — you can extend so much compassion to others in their grief, and yet when it comes to yourself, there's this inner voice calling it "self-indulgent," as if your love for your grandmother has an expiration date. Grief doesn't follow a schedule, and "barely functioning" after losing someone central to your life isn't a character flaw — it's a sign of how much she mattered. I'd gently ask: where do you think that rule came from, the one that says you should be "further along by now" — is that something you were taught, or a voice that's developed over time?

client: I think that voice has been there for a long time, honestly. My mom was never really one to sit with feelings — she'd always say things like "life goes on" or "you have to be strong," and I guess I absorbed that more than I realized. But hearing you say it out loud like that, that it came from somewhere, that it's not just the truth... I don't know, it's a little hard to fully believe, even if part of me wants to.
therapist: It sounds like something is quietly shifting in you even as you speak — that small part that *wants* to believe it didn't have to be this way is worth paying attention to, because it's been there underneath your mom's "be strong" message all along. You absorbed a rule that was never really yours to begin with, and recognizing that for the first time can feel both freeing and a little disorienting at the same time. I'm wondering — if you could gently begin to write your own rule about what it means to grieve, what would you want it to say?

client: I sit with that question for a moment, and honestly it makes me a little uncomfortable because I've never really thought about grief as something I get to define for myself. I think... maybe my rule would be that it's okay to feel sad without having to justify it or rush through it. But even saying that out loud feels kind of strange and almost selfish, like I'm giving myself permission I was never supposed to have.
therapist: What you just said — "it's okay to feel sad without having to justify it or rush through it" — that's not selfish, that's actually a profound act of self-compassion, and the fact that it feels strange is just the old rule putting up resistance. It makes sense that claiming something you were never given permission to have would feel uncomfortable at first, almost like you're breaking a family law that was never written down but always enforced. I'm curious — what would it feel like in your body, in your day-to-day life, if you actually started to live by that new rule you just created?

client: I sat with that question for a moment, and honestly, the first thing that came up was this weird mix of relief and fear at the same time. Like, if I actually let myself feel sad without rushing to justify it or fix it, I think there'd be this quieter kind of day... but I also worry it would just open up this huge space that I don't know how to fill. What if I let myself feel it and it just doesn't stop, you know?
therapist: That fear — "what if I let myself feel it and it just doesn't stop" — is one of the most common things people worry about when they first consider opening the door to grief, and it makes complete sense that it feels scary. But what you're also describing is something really hopeful: that alongside the fear, there's *relief*, which suggests part of you already senses that this sadness won't swallow you whole, even if it doesn't feel that way yet. I wonder if, in your experience so far, emotions — even the really big ones — have they ever actually lasted forever, or have they always eventually shifted in some way?

client: I mean... no, I guess they haven't lasted forever, not literally. But this one feels different somehow, like it's been sitting in my chest for so long that it's almost become part of me, and I'm not sure who I'd be without it. That probably sounds strange, but the grief over losing my dad has been there for two years now and I've just kind of... built my life around avoiding it.
therapist: It doesn't sound strange at all — it sounds like grief has quietly become a kind of companion, and there's something almost frightening about imagining life without it, like letting it go might mean losing another piece of your dad too. And I notice you've gently revealed something important just now — that this goes back even further, to your father, and that you've been carrying *two* losses while building your life around not fully feeling either of them. I'm wondering, when you say you've built your life around avoiding it, what has that cost you — what parts of yourself or your life do you feel like you've had to give up to keep that grief at a distance?

client: That question hits harder than I expected. I think I've given up... closeness, maybe? Like, I keep people at arm's length because if I let them in, I might actually feel things, and once I start feeling things I'm not sure I'd be able to stop. And somewhere along the way I think I also gave up on believing I deserved to be happy, because being happy felt like a betrayal of both of them.
therapist: What you just named is profound and tender — that somewhere in trying to protect yourself from the pain of losing them, you've also quietly closed the door on joy, connection, and your own worthiness of happiness. That belief, that being happy is a betrayal, is one of the heaviest things grief can leave behind, and I want you to know it makes complete sense that it developed, even as I gently want to challenge it. I'm wondering — do you think your dad or your grandmother, knowing how much you loved them, would actually want happiness to feel like a betrayal to you?
